scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9163: the NOC got a transient alert and now believes a core
backbone router (R6, possibly R7) "crashed and is down," and that traffic which
transits the core toward the far end of the network is being black-holed. They
want the crashed backbone router confirmed and recovered. Please confirm the fault.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R6 and R7 are up: their ospfd processes are
  running, the R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
  67.x, 70.x) are present in the backbone. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, so the core is forwarding. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone
  router crash that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r6-ospfd-down / kath5-r7-ospfd-down,
  where a core daemon IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a crashed backbone router
(R6/R7) black-holing core traffic -- is NOT reproducible: R6 and R7 are up, their
ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
67.x, 70.x) remain in the backbone. End to end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss, which requires the core to be forwarding -- inconsistent
with a crashed transit router on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the backbone routers are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks R6/R7 liveness (ospfd
running, adjacency Full, prefixes present) and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all
healthy -- and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a crashed router -- declaring
R6 or R7 down or restarting its frr to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
- Affected component: The routing control plane (FRR: ospfd/zebra) on core routers R6 and R7 restarted recently.
- Mechanism: The FRR restart tore down OSPF adjacencies and withdrew routes briefly, which would have transiently black-holed transit traffic and triggered the NOC alert. After daemons came back, OSPF neighbors re-formed and the FIB repopulated, restoring forwarding.
- Localization: On R6, OSPF neighbors to all three core links show short uptimes (Full with 14.1.4.1 on eth0 46.1.1.2, 15.1.4.1 on eth1 56.1.1.2, and 67.1.1.2 on eth2 67.1.1.1) at ~1 minute when checked. On R7, the OSPF neighbor to R6 on eth0 67.1.1.2 shows similar short uptime. Process start times confirm FRR was restarted about 2–3 minutes prior on both devices (r6 ospfd/zebra started at Sat Aug 1 19:21:58 UTC; r7 at 19:21:56), while the hosts themselves have been up for 3 days. Both FRR services are now active (running), OSPF is Full, and routing tables are populated. End-to-end reachability pc0→pc12 is 0% loss with ~1 ms RTT.
- Root cause: FRR daemons on R6 and R7 were restarted a few minutes ago (manual reload or crash), causing a brief routing outage, but the routers did not crash and are currently healthy.
- Corrective fix: No recovery action required now. To prevent recurrences, review FRR logs/core dumps (enable persistent journald), investigate why FRR restarted, and consider enabling systemd Restart=always and OSPF fast hellos/BFD to minimize convergence impact.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly states FRR services are active, OSPF is Full between R6/R7, and PC0→PC12 reachability is 0% loss, so the baseline healthy conditions are noted.

The agent's logs do show recent FRR/ospfd process start times and short OSPF neighbor uptimes (supporting a recent restart) and current reachability, but the key causal claim that the restart briefly black-holed transit traffic (triggering the NOC alert) is speculative and not directly evidenced (no route-withdrawal or journal entries shown). Overall the observations partly support the diagnosis but leave a critical gap tying the restart to an actual outage.
